utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. General --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I would like you to help us in understanding how you participated in coordinating the VJ and MUP anti-terrorist actions in 1998. And if I could start with the -- one of the items we looked at yesterday, it's Exhibit P1232. And I've got a hard copy of that if the usher would hand that to you. This is that 14 August 1998 decision concerning breaking up Siptar terrorist forces in the Slup and Voksa villages sector. Now, this involves tasks for both VJ units and MUP units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How would this information get from the Pristina Corps to the MUP? Can you tell the Judges how that worked. How did the MUP know what they were supposed to do and where they were supposed to be in carrying out this action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information was received at the level of the operations -- the operative organ of the Pristina Corps command and the operational and logistics department of the MUP staff; in other words, when a decision is adopted to use forces and when this decision is adopted or actually issued by the commander of the army and when he approves that decision, on the basis of that decision we would then proceed to coordinate and plan the activities foreseen. In other words, there would be an exchange of information and data, and also we would agree on the forces that are to be used in a certain operation. In other words, the MUP would determine what forces they need to use and what complements and the army would on their part also determine which forces to use in order to provide support to the MUP along a certain axis. Now, I have to explain something here. Coordination is to define cooperation and joint action in every aspect. This also means that there needs to be very precise coordination at all levels, not only at the staff level of the MUP and the Pristina Corps but also coordination at the level of combat groups and Special Police units and police detachments and other units. Would you like me to provide more detail? I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, once General Lazarevic had signed this decision and it was approved by General Samardzic, how did it get implemented in the field at that level? How did this information get from this document out to the troops who were going to carry out the action? If you could explain that process for us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume how it worked in Djakovica because I was not there in this particular -- on this particular occasion, but I know how we worked in Pristina. As a matter of principle, once a decision is made to break up forces within a certain area, once the MUP forces know where they will be used and the army forces know where they will be used, then we would proceed to coordinate the operation at a lower level, at the level of their employment. In other words, for instance, the units would be brought to a kilometre or two from the area where they are to be used, where the commander of the combat group and the supporting unit would meet. Now, usually they would be there together, but it's not necessarily so. And if they were not in the same spot together, then they would have to provide -- they would have to make sure that they had some means of communication, usually a Motorola would be used, a radio, a hand-held radio; and they could use these Motorolas in order to meet this criterion, in other words to provide communications with the army commander. But in most cases, both commanders were at the same spot and they would determine when support was needed, when the army needed to provide support to the MUP in a certain operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Take, for example, this document. Item 2.1 says that: "Battle group 15-3 is to support an attack of the 8th MUP Detachment and the Djakovica PJP ... along the following axes ..." And it describes a line from a certain village another village, et cetera. How did the 8th MUP Detachment and the Djakovica PJP get the information about where they were going to carry out the attack? Did they get a copy of this document? Did they get a map? How did they know, and where did that information come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would receive excerpts from the Pristina Corps as a basis for coordination. In other words, in order for them to be able to coordinate their action with army units, they would have had to receive a certain assignment. And when they are issued an assignment, the assignment is defined strictly as provided for, both for the unit that is participating in the action and the support unit, otherwise it would be impossible to coordinate their action. In other words, once they receive these excerpts, they would have to judge, assess, the situation in the same way that an army commander would do it, to see who was on their left flank, on the right flank, who was providing support in the rear, what kind of surprise they can expect. And based on that they would formulate their main action and decision. And on the basis of this, the MUP commander would use his own forces. Coordination, the purpose of coordination was only to make sure that no friendly fire came about to be, so that they would have to coordinate their participation, their action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. That makes sense to me. But where -- from where did the MUP -- the 8th MUP Detachment and the Djakovica PJP get the excerpt from this document? Who provided it to them? Did General Lazarevic send it to the 8th MUP Detachment? Did that come from your section? How did this information get from this document to the MUP detachment in the field? You said an excerpt of this document, so was it something that was copied or cut out and pasted? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 most documents were prepared at the Pristina Corps command as -- they were prepared as excerpts for police units. And it was also possible in the event that the -- General Lazarevic was at the Djakovica IKM, he could carry out those activities in the same manner that General Pavkovic, for instance, would do from Pristina because there was a part of command that was there with him who could actually carry out these tasks. And once an operation is completely coordinated and the final solution has been defined, then they would make excerpts from them that would relate to what the application or the employment of the MUP forces would be. And some of these items would be provided in short form in order for them to know where -- what the neighbouring units are, and other assignments would not be defined for the MUP units because they would have to define them themselves. That had to do -- that would usually relate to security, to providing medical assistance, to treatment of prisoners, wounded personnel, and so on. In other words, the tasks that the MUP defines for themselves, the same way that the army defines it for themselves. In other words, they would be provided with a certain number of assignments or some aspects of the assignments, and the other aspects they would have to define themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For those, those decisions that you helped work on, how did you deliver excerpts to the MUP concerning the tasks that they had to carry out? Who did you send it to and how did you transmit it, the excerpts for a MUP unit that was going to carry out an action in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were multiple participants, then we would have to coordinate via the staff because we could not issue the excerpts directly. But if it was a lower-intensity operation, then -- if General Lazarevic, for instance, was in Djakovica, he probably would not send this to Pristina again, but rather with the chief of the Ministry of the Interior in that territory he would probably coordinate the operation with him, which is quite in keeping with our regulations. In other words, it wasn't only the MUP staff that was in charge of coordination; coordination was also carried out at the level of secretariats, combat groups, detachments, all the way down to the lowest-level unit. So there were various versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Pristina you said that if it involved multiple participants, then you would coordinate via the staff. Do you mean the MUP staff at Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there a particular individual that you dealt with in forwarding these excerpts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as operations were concerned and the logistics part, for the most part I was in contact with Mr. Adamovic because I was referred to him by the MUP commander and Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall Mr. Adamovic's first name at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan, I believe his first name is Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the text, the excerpt from this decision, was there also a map that was delivered to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the excerpt the same way as the excerpts from the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could show you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document ID number D004-3062. This was not on my original list of documents I intended to show the witness, but the Defence this morning indicated to me that they planned to use it. I asked if I could go first and use it, and they had no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy, too, General, that I can hand you that may be easier for you to see than what's on the screen. Do you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a lower-level map, whereas the map that I would take to General Samardzic, it would relate to a wider area. So this would be an excerpt from the decision that was approved by the army commander, but I know that for these joint operations at Voksa were -- I know that it was approved, but I did not see this one because it was at the Djakovica IKM, whereas the one that General Samardzic approved, the one that I took to General Samardzic to approve, it also included the villages of Stup, Voks and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see in the upper left-hand corner what appears to be the name and the signature of General Samardzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once he approved - I've already explained this procedure - he would use a highlighter to approve that decision. He would use -- and this one here was -- as far as I can see, it was a simple pen, felt pen. But I know that he would usually approve such decisions in the same way that you see the pen that is used for General Pavkovic at the bottom. So he would approve the excerpt from this portion and probably he was -- somebody took this to him to also approve this because he would approve everything. And I'm sure that he approved the operation Voks and Stup and the use of the forces there. The last time I had another map which was the original map. The last time you showed me the original map that I took to them for approval. Now this is something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't -- I don't recall what map we showed you last time, but this -- this does appear to be a map related to that decision signed by General Lazarevic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Because we see on the map what appears to be the designation for the 8th MUP Detachment and for Battle Group 15-3, et cetera, around the area of Slup; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. That's all I needed to ask you about that right now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Voksa --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke. Voksa.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this relates to Voksa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you say this was a lower-level map, so is this what the MUP unit, the 8th MUP Detachment would have in hand, a map like this, to see where they were supposed to be, or would it be something even smaller?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, lastly I want to talk about -- well, two topics. The first is MUP subordination to the VJ or lack thereof. You're aware, aren't you, General, that during the war there was an issue about whether or not the MUP should be subordinated to the VJ for purposes of combat? You knew about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it there was a constitutional provision that allowed for that to take place; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the VJ General Staff or General Ojdanic ever issue any order to try and have that take effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff attempted to do that. There was an order from the 18th of April, I believe, that was received on the 18th of April, and that decision did not come to be implemented because the explanation that was given was that the organs of the Ministry [as interpreted] of the Interior did not receive an identical order from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia as superior officers at the ministry. That was the explanation provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask some more questions about that. But before I forget, can I tender D004-3062 of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01237.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could we see -- oh, I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. The witness said that organs of the ministry had not received orders from the minister, that's what it should say, not from the ministry, so from the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If next we could see Exhibit -- or 65 ter number 01267. If I could show you a hard copy -- well, I see the whole page is on the screen, so if we could just have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated the 20th of April, 1999, from General Lazarevic to his subordinate units. And he's ordering units and organs of the MUP to be resubordinated to the VJ brigade command. And do you see the first paragraph in this order where it says: "Pursuant to the order by the Supreme Command Staff" it cites the number "of 18 April, 1999, and an announcement of the 3rd Army command of the 20th of April," he's issuing this order. So it appears you were right, it was the 18th of April that there was an order of the Supreme Command for this subordination to take place. Did you ever see General Lazarevic's order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware -- I know of this order and I also subsequently saw an order that had arrived from the General Staff of the army to Pristina Corps, sent to Pristina Corps to do with resubordination. And I also know of this order from General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also see the order that General Pavkovic had sent out passing on basically the order from the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is -- that was done within the army, and I was already within the army at this time as an operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it appears in the list of addressees at the very bottom of the order - we'll have to see page 2 of the English - that this order from General Lazarevic also went to the Pristina MUP staff. Do you see there -- do you see that listed? I think it's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, after you -- well, where were you on the 20th of April physically located, or the 18th/19th of April, whenever the order first came down to where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, General Pavkovic received this dispatch; on the 19th I remember that I wrote an order that had to do -- that dealt with refugees and some other matters; and on the 20th I was probably also physically there. I can't recall with certainty that there was any special thing that I did then, but I know that for sure that on these days I was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I move on could I tender 01267 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01238.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After this order from General Ojdanic was received, did you or General Pavkovic have any contact with the MUP about how this was going to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a contact sometime in the afternoon. I spoke about this at a trial last year. It was around 1700 or 1730 hours. We were in a room, I think in the building of Kosovska Banka or somewhere else because at the time we had to move around because of the air-strikes. A few officers and us were sitting there. At one point a group of officers from the MUP entered the room, the ones from Pristina, and they joined us at the desk where we, five or six officers of us from the Pristina Corps, were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take this step by step. This meeting took place at this -- you think it was in the bank of Kosova. That was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Pristina, and I believe it was the bank building, but I'm not quite sure, but definitely in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the meeting took place on the same day that you had received the Supreme Command Staff order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who arranged the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information about any impending meeting because General Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and I and other officers were conducting some informal conversation. We gathered together, and I think that General Pavkovic then informed someone from the MUP staff or some officer from the police, and that subsequently they came to this room where we already were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who from the VJ was in the room when this meeting took place? You mentioned yourself and General Pavkovic. Who else was present that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely remember General Lazarevic being there and maybe another two or three colonels, but at this point I'm not quite sure. I'm only sure about General Lazarevic, Pavkovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who from the MUP came in and participated in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Lukic, and Mr. Obrad Stevanovic were the persons from the MUP who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened at the meeting? Who started talking first and what about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the gentlemen from the Ministry of the Interior arrived, they sat next to each other, and General Pavkovic, since General Djordjevic sat next to him, he handed him the telegram for him to read it without explaining anything. Now, whether they had heard about this previously or not, I don't know; all I know is he gave him the telegram to read. Maybe after a minute or so, because it was a short telegram, Mr. Djordjevic gave the telegram back to General Pavkovic and added, What do you mean Ojdanic? Who does he think he is that he can command? There will be no subordination until we receive such an instruction, an order, from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the telegram you're referring to is the one that you had received from General Ojdanic and the Supreme Command Staff? That's the one that was handed --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Resubordination, not subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that remark from General Djordjevic, what happened next in the meeting? Did you have any further discussion about the issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally somewhat surprised because I had no knowledge about the telegram to begin with, and we never expected this issue to be raised. Secondly, there were no comments on the part of other organs. Some informal conversation lasted for a couple of minutes, and after that we split without having defined anything because basically prior to that there had been no problems during the conducting of the operations. The main problem was the issue of resubordination and the reason why this did not happen was simply the absence of the order from the minister instructing the police to do so. So that applied to the whole period of 1998, which meant that there could be no action without specific order from the MUP commander and the persons in charge, which only makes sense, and this is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in spite of that did the MUP -- did the VJ, after 18, 19, 20 of April, continue to issue orders that contemplated MUP being subordinated to the VJ? Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. It's clear. There were attempts at all levels to define this by means of an order pursuant to General Lazarevic's order. Equally, the same applied to brigade commanders. This was not only the problem at the MUP staff level, but it was a problem also within the PJP and other units that could have been resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look next at 65 ter number 01269. I can give you a hard copy of this one. This is dated the 8th of May, 1999, from General Pavkovic concerning the deployment of VJ and MUP forces in combat and control of the territory, an order. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have and I am the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you explained before on the last page, directly across from General Pavkovic's signature and stamp, we see your initials followed by a slash and someone else's initials. Is it correct that the initials of the person on the left are the one who drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first initials MDj is the author, in this particular case it was me, and this other person was the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in this order it appears that Pavkovic is trying to direct how MUP units are going to be deployed for certain purposes. And I see handwritten at the top it says: "Pristina MUP to General Lukic personally ..." Do you know who wrote that in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written by General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know if it was delivered to General Lukic personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I did, however, warned the general that they were not going to carry this out, but he replied, It's up to us to forward this to them. That was his only comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 1269.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received with the official translation we have. There is another translation which is not official.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01239.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, I'd like us to look at 65 ter number 01723. I can give you a hard copy of this one as well. This is dated the 24th of May, 1999, from General Lazarevic to General Pavkovic as the commander of the 3rd Army. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it while it was being drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, it was Vladimir Lazarevic himself and this must be accurate because General Lazarevic was in the habit of quickly writing reports in order not to waste time, because he thought that, just like General Pavkovic, he could explain certain things much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you'll go down under the order to the fifth bullet point where it talks about the work of mixed check-points of the MUP and military police. Do you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in there that he talks about there are problems and salient issues since the MUP tolerates criminal activities of its members against the Siptar civilian population, murder, rape, looting, robbery, and so on. Were you aware of that problem -- were you personally aware of that problem on the 24th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to this extent. There were certain incidents of the kind, but as for rape -- I know that there were thefts; I know that there were car thefts and thefts of household appliances. There were some isolated cases, but here you don't see the scale and the extent of this. If they say just rape, it would be two rapes or 50 rapes. And by the way, this particular issue was not within my purview and my area of interest, and I was not in charge of following these developments. I may have heard something during the briefing at the command, but that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't know where General Lazarevic got his information from that led him to write that in his report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't. I can only assume that he received it either from the commanders or from his assistants, and that is to say security organs. So it either came from the commanding officers or he got it from a security organ. I don't believe that he personally witnessed all these events because he would have then formulated it in a different way, in a completely different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender 1723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01240.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next one if we could look at Exhibit P888, already in evidence, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I can give you a hard copy of this next one as well. And this one, you'll see, is the very next day. And this one is from General Pavkovic. By the initials it looks like he, himself, was the author. And it's to the Supreme Command Staff concerning subordination or resubordination of the MUP. Did you see this document back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, while it was being drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he, too - I think it's in item 3 on the first page - passes on information about problems at the joint check-points and that the MUP members condone or openly permit evident criminal activities and plunder committed by their fellow MUP members as well as civilians resulting in appropriation of vehicles, et cetera. And on the next page in item 4 he talks about the noncompliance with resubordination, and he goes on to say: " ... some MUP members and to a considerable extent entire smaller units, which 'operate' independently on the ground are committing serious crimes against the Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee shelters - murder, rape, plunder, robbery, ..." Now, do you know where General Pavkovic was getting his information? Was it based solely on the report he had gotten the day before from General Lazarevic, or did he have some additional source?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that his main source was General Lazarevic's report, because General Pavkovic did not have enough personnel from the army command in order to cover these issues. These issues were mainly covered by the section that was part of the Pristina Corps, that is to say subordinate commands and security organs and command organs who were capable, first, of feeding information to General Lazarevic; and subsequently, General Pavkovic probably acquired the same information as the one that was written and recorded by General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last thing I'd like you to look at in this document is the last paragraph called: "Measures Proposed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he is urging the Supreme Command to take urgent measures falling within its jurisdiction to resubordinate the units and organs of the MUP in the spirit of the Constitution and existing laws in accordance with the proclaimed state of war or, otherwise, annul the order on the resubordination and then: "... leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior - Staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija through the Joint Command as has so far been the case." So it seems that on May 25th, 1999, General Pavkovic at least is under the impression that the MUP units have been commanded through this body called the Joint Command; that's what it says. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djurdjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please stop. My learned friend Mr. Hannis arrived at a conclusion that does not derive from what he has just read. I wouldn't like to go any further in belabouring this issue, but if you think that I am right, then I would kindly ask for your indulgence to allow me to explain. I think that the conclusion is quite the opposite to the one reached by Mr. Hannis judging by the citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, this appears to be a material point. I think it is a matter to be dealt with by cross-examination if you take a different view. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you need me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is - and given that I attended the meetings of the Joint Command and this part which refers to the general's proposal to annul the order, which is only logical. He says either to annul the order or to continue to implement coordination and separate planning and actions by the MUP and the army, but under the coordination with the coordination - and I always add mutual coordination - of the Joint Command. If this order is annulled, then the previous practice could continue separately with coordination, but each segment would be responsible for their respective tasks and units. This is what General Pavkovic had in mind. So that was the practice that was applied before because the MUP organs had not been subordinated to the army units. He proposes that this situation can continue, but in that event the corps cannot assume responsibility for the actions of other participants in the zone unless they are subordinated to the Pristina Corps. This was the idea of General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did he tell you that personally, or are you just assuming that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because the two of us had frequent contacts. I am fully familiar with how he thinks and what his views were. He did not mind the fact that the MUP was not subordinated, but he did not want to take responsibility for something that he cannot give orders for, and it only is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I agree, that's reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we next look at 65 ter number 01281. If we could look at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the -- this is from the VJ web site on the internet on the 14th of June, 2001. And have you seen this before? Did -- was this shown to you previously?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the briefing, and I am aware of the events that are described here and I learned about them from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the bottom of the B/C/S page, the big paragraph there is the one I want to focus on. And for English we actually have to go over to the next page, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're aware that around this time in 2001 that there was some public debate or discussion between General Pavkovic and the then-Minister of the Interior, Dusan Mihajlovic, that centred around the publicity concerning the freezer trucks with bodies that had been found in the river during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the minister of the interior had made some allegations suggesting that the army had been involved or perhaps involved in that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you'll look at that paragraph 4, about halfway through the paragraph, General Pavkovic is talking about how -- it's translated here in the English as: " ... it is true that the national defence law regulated that police units in the responsibility zones were bound to subordinate to the commands of the Yugoslav Army. However, this never came into existence ..." And you agree with that, right, the MUP never was actually subordinated to the VJ in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not in the classical sense as one would understand the meaning of resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you'll be patient and follow along with me just a little bit more. He goes on to say: "The Police had their own headquarters, headed by their own officers, and the cooperation with the Army was coordinated through political actors in Joint Command, formed for the purpose. Therefore, the information to what the police force units were doing can best be provided by the police commanders and the members of the Joint Command in charge of them." Now, General Pavkovic seems to be suggesting that Joint Command included political actors.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the text reads, and this is how he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this text is completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this was posted on the VJ web site. You have no reason to believe that that's not correct? You never heard of General Pavkovic coming out and denying he said this, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the meaning is accurate, but I cannot vouch say for every sentence being accurate. I'm not expressing any doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this document being admitted. This is a site that was taken off another site, and the witness is providing an opinion of something that he learned from the press. He doesn't even know whether this article is correct and accurate. He said that the spirit is there but he cannot guarantee for the accuracy of the comments, and I think that this kind of documents and exhibits should be introduced through someone else, not through this witness. This site was taken off another site in 2001. How this took place, whether this is an official site or an unofficial site and who did that, I don't know; therefore, it makes this totally unreliable. And I particularly object to the witness giving his opinion about what he is not quite sure and on what he has not sufficient knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive this document. Some of the matters raised by Mr. Djurdjic may in time be relevant to weight when the Chamber comes to assess the nature of the document, but on its face there is a sufficient indication of reliability and the knowledge of the witness at the time is sufficient in the Chamber's view to support the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01241.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I just have three more items to show you and these all are sort of matters of general information about the VJ in 1998 and 1999. The first one I wanted to show you is 65 ter number 02556. I think we have this in English only I believe, but this is a document that was shown to you during proofing. And my question for you: Does this document accurately reflect the organisational structure within the VJ in 1999 -- because it shows General Ojdanic as the Chief of the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff. Does it accurately reflect all the VJ units that were under General Lazarevic in the Pristina Corps in 1999? I don't know if you're able to read it on the screen. Do we need to enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could you just enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that any better for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better. This is an organigram that reflects the structure, but I would have to make some corrections. General Pavkovic is the Pristina Military District; and where it says Zlatomir Pesic as the commander, he was actually resubordinated to General Lazarevic in April and they were under the immediate direct command of General Lazarevic. And he also resubordinated parts of the detachment to the brigade commander. So he was the command of the army in 1998, and he commanded directly with the military district of Pristina, but as of April 1999 he actually ceded the command to General Lazarevic and the commander of the Pristina Corps. That would be my intervention here. Now, as for the second, the commander of the 15th Armoured Brigade, that's correct; 125th, correct; 243rd Mechanised, correct; 549th Motorised, correct; 52th Mixed Artillery, correct; 52nd Mixed Air Defence and Rocket Artillery Brigade, correct; 37th -- I think it's the 37th, Djikovic, yes, that's the brigade that was resubordinated from Raska to General Lazarevic. In other words, it is not an establishment unit; it was just resubordinated for the purposes of combat operations in Kosovo. The 354th is our unit of the Pristina Corps. The 58th also the establishment unit. 175th is the resubordinated brigade from the Nis Corps. The 7th Brigade was also resubordinated from Krusevac. The 211th was another Nis Corps unit which was resubordinated. The 252nd, I cannot quite make out what unit this is referring to, 252nd --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says armoured brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, armoured, yes. That was also a unit that was added to or joined to this. And the 72nd Brigade, I remember -- well, you actually asked me during the proofing session, and then I subsequently recollected that General Perisic did not approve the resubordination of the entire 72nd Brigade, but only the scout company and, I believe, a police unit, reinforced company, or something of that level. And he kept this as a reserve, although --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer referring to whom it was resubordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear the interpreter? There was a request that you repeat the last portion of your answer referring to whom it was resubordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 72nd Special Brigade was not, in its full complement, part of the Pristina Corps. General Pavkovic asked General Ojdanic to resubordinate the entire 72nd Special Brigade to him. And the reply he received in writing was that this was not approved, not the resubordination of the entire 72nd Special Brigade because there was already a scout unit as part of the corps from the 72nd Brigade and another unit of the rank of a reinforced company up to the level of battalion of the police complement. The 63rd Parachute Brigade only participated with one unit, one combat unit -- one combat group both in 1998 and 1999. The 52nd Military Police Battalion, this is an establishment unit of the Pristina Corps. The same is true of the 52nd -- I don't know if this is the medical unit. I know that it exists, but I'm not sure. I can't really make out what this here stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In English it says "reconnaissance and diversionary company."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, right, reconnaissance or scout company. Yes, I couldn't read that, I couldn't see it. Yes, that's also a unit that is part of the establishment of the Pristina Corps. Then we have the 53rd Border Guards Battalion, that's a battalion that was on the border with the Republic of Albania, the 55th Border Guards Battalion, the same is true of this. And the 75th Border Guards Battalion was on the border with the Republic of Macedonia. These were the border guards battalions of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I move to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01242.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, General, 65 ter number 01548. This was another document I think you were shown during proofing, and in the English translation it's: "Rule on official correspondence and office administration in the Army of Yugoslavia." Are you familiar with this document from 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this? Was this sort of your style book in the army about how correspondence was to be drafted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is -- it provides very in -- with a lot of precision for how a document is to be drafted, how it is going to be filed, what form it has to follow. So this is an instruction that was implemented by the organ that was in charge of these activities, and they were part of my department, the department that I was at the head of as of 1998 in the Pristina Corps. And the head of that department was a junior officer who's in charge of implementing these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this the version of the rule that was in effect in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were still following this rule because we had not been provided the new rule, so this was implemented and in force both in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I move to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01243.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour. I have one more document I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lastly, General, I would like to show you 65 ter number 01739. General, this is another one that you were shown during proofing, and it's a list of -- it's a purported list of members of the VJ General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff, I guess, during the first sixth months of 1999. And can you have a look at it and confirm for us whether or not to your knowledge those people were on the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff during the wartime in the positions that are named there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ojdanic was there. He was the Chief of the General Staff. His deputy was General Marjanovic. I know this for a fact. Now, I don't know Mr. Arsenovic, I haven't met him, but I know of him and the name rings a bell, but what position exactly he was at, I I'm not really sure. It says here that he was advisor, but I don't know him personally. Obradovic, Milorad and Kovacevic, Blagoje, that's true, they were assistant Chiefs of the General Staff or operations of staff matters. And Panic, Miodrag and Simic, Miodrag assistant Chiefs of the General Staff for the land army, I know both men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assistant Chief of the General Staff of the air force and PVO, those assistant chiefs were General Grahovac, General Velickovic, and General Karanovic. I know the individuals, some of them I know personally, and I know all the names. The assistant Chief of the General Staff for the navy, Vlado Nonkovic, I know him, this is correct. Assistant Chief of the General Staff for communications, information technology, and electronic war fair, Ljubomir Andjelkovic, I know the man. Assistant Chief of the General Staff for recruitment, mobilisation, and system matters, Risto Matovic, I know the person. Assistant Chief of the General Staff for logistics, Vidoje Pantelic, I also know this man. Assistant Chief of the General Staff for education training, Sinisa Borovic and Zlatoje Terzic, I know both men. The chief of the Yugoslav Army inspectorate of the Yugoslav army, General Samardzic, the former commander of the 3rd Army, I know him. He was later appointed to the post of inspector in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if there's another page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so -- actually, there is. The chief of the information and moral guidance administration, General Zivanovic, I know him. And as for Aleksandar Bakocevic, I don't know him. It says here that he's a reserve major general, I don't know him in person. The chief of the housing administration, Spasoje Djurovic, I know him. And Miodrag Panic, lieutenant-general, I think that his name appears twice here, as far as I could observe. There was a Panic together with General Simic. I think it's the same Panic, Miodrag Panic. I think his name is duplicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you'll see -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, the chief of the security administration and Geza Farkas, his deputy. The chief of the intelligence administration, General Krga, I know all these men. And the chief of the first administration, Djordje Curcin, I know him. In other words, the only thing that remains to be clarified is the name of Miodrag Panic. Maybe he appears twice because here it says as of April 2nd, 1999, and maybe earlier it appeared until or before April 2nd, 1999, in that case, it's correct. In any case, I know all these generals mentioned here. Some of them are no longer living, two or three, whereas most of the others have retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with that I have no more questions for the General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time for a break do you think, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break a little early and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, and I'm a member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. With me together in the team today are Ms. Marie O'Leary and Mr. Aleksandar Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since we speak the same language and you are a very fast speaker and when I get carried away I get to speak even faster, I appeal to you in order to get a correct interpretation and a clean transcript, please bear in mind that we should keep our speed under control which is better than to go back and correct portions of the testimony. Now, General, let me ask you first, after you completed the military academy, what military schools did you attend and which army did those academies belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1971 I completed the infantry academy. And in 1881 [as interpreted] until 1883 I attended and completed the command staff academy, it's a two-year school. And in 1990 through 2000 I completed the National Defence college or school. So practically I completed all military schools that existed in the army of the SFRY and the Army of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your specialty is infantry; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit, or rather, document 65 ter 02088.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order issued by the commander of the Pristina Corps dated the 29th of May, 1998. What I would like to ask you is you're familiar with the format of this document, but are you also familiar with the content of the document? Were you familiar with it at the time when it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is: What was the political situation like, what was the backdrop, and what was it that led to such an order being issued?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political and security situation at this time was extremely complex. The fact that the army command issued this order to the command of the Pristina Corps to which it refers to place at full combat-readiness the entire standing complement of the Pristina Corps up until the 29th of May, 1998, and it further describes and defines other issues that are of lesser significance. But what is most important here is that it was necessary to raise to full combat-readiness the composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you please now just tell us in lay terms what combat-readiness or full combat-readiness, rather, means.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I have to say an order to raise to full combat-readiness can be issued by a superior command at the level of the General Staff. And the measures and procedures of -- applicable to units and individuals when the -- when we have this situation of raising to full combat-readiness is prescribed by them. The full combat-readiness means that certain measures and actions of individuals and units should be made according to certain levels of combat-readiness, various levels of combat readiness. And at one point all units have to be at this level of full combat-readiness; in other words, ready and prepared for any situation that may occur in the territory where the unit is deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please tell us a bit about the political and security situation that demanded the raising to full combat-readiness of the units.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, on the 29th of May, 1998, this is the time when in the border area there were already combat -- combat -- there was already fighting with terrorist Siptar forces which attempted in various ways to bring weapons and equipment to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija through armed force. Also, in the rear outside the area of the border area they were taking up position at major intersections, crossroads, dominant elevations, organise -- they had to organise defence and prepare features for the protection of personnel and to provide for the Defence of settlements. And they were terrorising and attacking the civilian population. And in this period of time they were especially focused on targeting members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, would you agree with my assessment, with my statement, that the purpose and the objective of the Albanian separatists was to secede, or rather, to cut off Kosovo and Metohija through armed force from the Serbia and Yugoslavia; is -- was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that we enter this into evidence, Your Honours. I move that we admit this document into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00318.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have Defence document D004-3002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a decision of the commander of the 3rd Army to establish a forward command post. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are the reasons mentioned here, were they the reason for the commander's decision to establish a forward command post in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you now please explain this. Could the army commander issue this decision independently, or would he have done this on orders of the chief of the -- Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not do this independently. In order to establish any command post, a junior -- or rather, a subordinate officer could not establish such a command post without an order from his superior. And let me just say this, I know as a fact that General Pavkovic informed us that General Samardzic at a meeting with President Milosevic proposed that his men establish an -- a forward command post in the barracks in Pristina. And then I asked him, What did the president reply to that? And he said -- well, he didn't say anything. He just went over that. So we considered that to be approved. That was the gist of his comment. And later on as I went through certain documents I confirmed this. So this is an activity that could not be carried out by the -- by an army commander without at least a -- an approval from the Chief of Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you have referred to this -- to meetings with the president of the republic on several occasions during your testimony. Would it be more precise to say at meetings of the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was a meeting with the president because it was held at the president's premises. He is the supreme commander, and it is within his competence to command the army in war and peacetime. Whether the meeting would be held in -- at the federal -- at the Executive Council or the Beli Dvor, that was irrelevant, but this would be a meeting where he would convene a meeting and invite officers to come and join him. So the Supreme Defence Council actually approved the use of the army at the meeting that was held with the president, and the president, President Milosevic, issued tasks to his subordinate officers, or rather, to General Perisic in -- for the army with the presence of General Samardzic, Pavkovic, and so forth, and also in the presence of the minister of the interior and his subordinate officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned the minister of the interior, am I correct that these meetings of the Supreme Defence Council were also attended by the president of the Republic of Serbia, at the time Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00319.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, let us clarify this. In addition to this proposal being made at the meeting with the chairman of the Supreme Defence Council, was an approval required to be given to General Samardzic to set up the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they had prior agreement before this meeting with the president, that is to say to send a team of officers of the 3rd Army to be sent to Pristina in order to provide support to the 3rd Corps [as interpreted], in view of the tasks and the higher level of alert and combat-readiness. Whether General Perisic gave only oral approval or if he gave it in writing, I don't know. It is possible in the military to accept an oral approval and it is considered to be valid, but as a matter of principle it should be always followed by a written approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 3, page 36, it should read Pristina Corps rather than the 3rd Corps. That is actually line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit P1216.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are again reminded to pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you're now going to see a document already shown to you by Mr. Hannis, and you made some comments on it. It is an order issued by the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade, dated July 7th, 1998. Let me first ask you this: As far as I was able to understand, in your conversation with Mr. Pavkovic earlier in the beginning of July -- June, you agreed to call certain coordinating activities as the activities of the Joint Command. Did I understand that properly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely. I still believe that much before the arrival of civilians to the territory of Kosovo, I even never imagined that anyone would come. At my proposal to the general and in order to make this coordination official, we used to write it as K and M Joint Command. You can see that clearly under item 2 which says that MUP unit and the army shall be approved by the MUP and the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell me, what were the activities that at the time you qualified as the ones to be carried out by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking I remember, I believe that these activities identified as something to be carried out by the Joint Command were under somewhat altered name of the operation that was conducted by the Ministry of the Interior in the area between Pec-Djakovica-Prizren road in order to lift the blockade on this road. This operation was called Grom. It was considered that this was directed by an inter-departmental staff, and after that we started with this Joint Command because this inter-departmental staff led by Mr. Stanisic was somehow disband because they were not up to the tasks that had been planned and due to that these changes took place. It all took place in June 1998. The general accepted my proposal, and we started making documents with the heading "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please slow down so that we can get correct translation and transcript. It says here that this is document number 1104-6 -- actually, reference is made to this document. At the time when this number 6 was added, was that in compliance with the register that just by random appears as number 6 under which a decision is recorded where this is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask again the speakers to slow down and to pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Coordination within the MUP and the army because at the time there were no civilians. Coordination was implemented exclusively between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When this situation happened, did you as the head of the operations department initiated a contact for the first time with the MUP in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can say so. I would say that it was a first time, although there had been some contacts in passing when General Perisic used to come down there in April and May, and we were under the obligation to contact the MUP organs, but all of this was in a certain manner prompted by the need to make preparations for the arrival of General Perisic in Kosovo. I can say that more intensive contacts with the MUP started in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the MUP at the time when you coordinated these actions on behalf of the Pristina Corps during these activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in late June General Pavkovic mentioned General Lukic to me as the MUP staff commander. And for the first time I met General Lukic face-to-face on the 22nd of July at the meeting where all the other senior officers from the MUP were present. And we may have had some meetings with some other organs, but these were informal conversations without going into many details and problematic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the document under 65 ter number 04038.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is information provided by the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to the federal minister of foreign affairs of the FRY on the 16th of July, 1998. Were you aware of this document? Did you ever hear of it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As for the format, is it familiar to you? Does it resemble the format used by the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is fully in compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise Mr. Perisic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll down the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was seldom in a position to see Mr. Perisic in person because he was my second superior in hierarchy. I can recognise the signatures of General Samardzic and General Pavkovic, but I never had an opportunity to see Mr. Perisic's signature. But since there is a stamp, I have no doubts about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This information contains some attachments. One refers to involvement of the Republic of Albania and the events in Kosovo, list of weapons, ammunition and other military equipment, and list of Yugoslav army soldiers killed and wounded in Kosovo and Metohija during 1998. The information that were received by the General Staff through the 3rd Army, did it contain information that the Republic of Albania provided their territory for the terrorists' training, that they provided support in providing weapons to them, and that the Ministry of the Interior and other authorities of the Republic of Albania were involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs who were charged with monitoring the security situation close to the border, as far as I know, had some information about the involvement of the Republic of Albania and the events in Kosovo, primarily following the events that took place in the Republic of Albania relating to the looting of weapons from depots in the northern part of Albania in the area of Kukes, Tropoja, et cetera. There was a lot of information to that effect, and I believe that the intelligence and security organs from Kosovo provided the competent authorities with this kind of reports, and suppose that these services were -- by their function were obliged to provide this to General Perisic. And then General Perisic would forward this information to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It should be corrected, minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the same reasons that we gave in respect of a number of Prosecution documents that were subject of objection today, this will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00320.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, let us now go back to your yesterday's conversation with Mr. Hannis about the plan for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. Did I understand you correctly when you said that you took part in creating this plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in charge of this job on behalf the Pristina Corps, and this was my functional duty. At that point, I was the person who was involved this, of course under the supervision of General Pavkovic, and on the basis of the -- of information received by General Lazarevic and other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This proposal of a plan that you made in the Pristina Corps, was it presented to the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I suppose it was. I know that President Milosevic saw it, and definitely if the Supreme Council decided to implement this plan, then it only makes sense that the plan had been previously presented to the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the elements contained in this proposal of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already mentioned these elements contained in the plan, but I can amend it by saying the following in view of your question. I said that initially it was comprised of three stages. The first stage involved the engagement of border units of the army in the border area. The police had no jurisdiction there except for their regular policing and checking the movement of people and vehicles. The major factor there, preventing the incursion of terrorist forces and their retreating to Albania for training and arming, was under the jurisdiction of the army. The next or the second phase involved the engagement of MUP units and support provided by the army in the process of breaking up terrorist forces along the main road between Pec, Djakovica, and Prizren. And in the process of drawing up this plan and in line with the rules governing the preparation of working map which requires plans to be made and various signs to be included for various structures such as the army and the MUP and the Ministry of Defence and all other forces that are included in the plan, we plotted roughly on the map the MUP unit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The units of the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- without any specific annotations attached to these units, because at the time the ministry defined its own tasks relating to the preparation of this plan. At the time we still didn't know which units from the ministry were to take place, but we nevertheless marked them with colour green without specifying the names because we were still waiting for the plan to be incorporated from the MUP staff. And the third phase also involved support to the MUP forces in lifting the blockade of the roads, of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You already said that. Let us not repeat things. Please, according to your knowledge, was this plan, as you proposed it, ever adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was adopted. Once we received information from the MUP staff about which units are going to take part, we included this information into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let us clarify one thing. What you told me so far and after having reading many documents, I found out that this was called a global plan for the destruction of sabotage and terrorist forces in Kosovo. So that entailed that at a later stage detailed plans would be drawn up according to specific activities envisaged in the global plan; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that following this stage what we saw here were your decisions, your instructions and directives, referring to certain actions that were envisaged in this global plan in these various stages. You're free to correct me if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, following this we would look at the excerpts from the global plan which only provide the basic elements for us to be able to plan combat operations, both at the level of the army and the MUP, and in coordination between these two structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please just correct something, on page 42, line 13, when you mentioned various forces, General, we see here in the transcript the Ministry of Defence. Is that what you actually said, or did you refer to the forces of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which part of my testimony you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, talking about this general plan and what the units entered in green ink were representing, what did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, based on this global plan, then there would be various decisions and orders issued for various stages of the operation. And it was at this level that there would be a degree of coordination between the Pristina Corps and the MUP staff in Pristina. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And at this stage politicians would also join this process of coordination, and as far as I understood you, this happened for the first time on the 22nd of July, 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the 22nd of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And on this day a meeting was held, am I correct, where as you mentioned you started making notes for your own use?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first time that I saw these persons and I mentioned already, I wrote down the names of the individuals that I knew and also the ones that I didn't. Up until then I had no contact whatsoever with these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already explained all this, but now let me ask you this: Did you ever see any kind of decision on the establishment of a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Or the composition of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, in view of this first minutes of the meeting and you mentioned there the individuals who were present. Now, in addition to these individuals who were -- whose names were entered in the first minutes, could you tell us what other individuals came to these joint meetings, the meetings of the Joint Command, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some 20 or so individuals who would attend these meetings, 20 to 23, 22 or 23 individuals. Most of these people were from state security and then from the Ministry of the Interior and from the ministry -- the defence ministry. And I remember that from the security -- from the state security there was the chief of state security for Pristina, I believe his name was Zlakovic [phoen] or something like that, but he was the chief of state security. I think Radovic was absent as well as Gajic, and that he actually was standing in for them. I'm pretty sure that he was there as the chief for Pristina.
